<div class="accordion-item"><h2 class="accordion-header"><button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#work-acc-summary">Summary</button></h2><div id="work-acc-summary" class="accordion-collapse collapse"><div class="accordion-body">Mahāvīrācārita is an epic poem written by the 8th-century Indian poet Bhavabhūti. It consists of 28 chapters and is written in Sanskrit. The epic revolves around the life of Mahāvīra, the 24th and last Tirthankara (spiritual teacher) of Jainism. It begins with a description of the Jain cosmology, including the various realms of existence and the concept of karma. The story then moves on to the birth and early life of Mahāvīra. Mahāvīra was born in a royal family in Kundagrāma (modern- day Bihar, India) and was named Vardhamāna. The poem describes his early life as a prince and his decision to renounce his worldly life in search of spiritual enlightenment. He spends 12 years as an ascetic, practicing austerities and meditation, and finally attains enlightenment under a Sal tree, which is now known as the Jaina Stupa. The poem also describes Mahāvīra's teachings and his establishment of the Jain community. It recounts various incidents from his life, such as his encounters with other religious leaders, his travels, and his interactions with his disciples. The epic ends with Mahāvīra's attainment of moksha (liberation from the cycle of rebirth).</div></div></div>

<div class="accordion-item"><h2 class="accordion-header"><button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#work-acc-uniqueness">Uniqueness</button></h2><div id="work-acc-uniqueness" class="accordion-collapse collapse"><div class="accordion-body">is a unique work in several aspects. Firstly, it is one of the few surviving Sanskrit plays that deals with Jain themes and characters, providing valuable insights into the Jain culture and beliefs of ancient India. Secondly, the play showcases the author's mastery over the Sanskrit language and poetry, as well as his ability to create complex characters and plotlines. Thirdly, the Mahāvīrācārita is unique in its portrayal of the character of Mahāvīra, who is depicted as a compassionate and wise teacher, rather than a divine figure. This humanization of Mahāvīra makes the play more relatable and inspiring to the audience. Finally, the Mahāvīrācārita also serves as a historical record of the social and political conditions of ancient India, providing a glimpse into the lives of people during that era.</div></div></div>
<div class="accordion-item"><h2 class="accordion-header"><button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#work-acc-contribution">Contribution &amp; Notes</button></h2><div id="work-acc-contribution" class="accordion-collapse collapse"><div class="accordion-body">is considered a significant contribution to Sanskrit literature for its excellent storytelling, use of language, and philosophical insights. The work presents a vivid picture of ancient Indian society and the Jain religion's principles and practices. Bhavabhūti's mastery of language and literary techniques, such as the use of metaphor and imagery, is evident throughout the text, making it a masterpiece of Sanskrit poetry. The work's philosophical themes, including karma, rebirth, and non-violence, make it an essential contribution to the Jain religious tradition's philosophical literature.</div></div></div>
